title: Imperfect World Models are Exploitable
claim: A model's value function can be trivial, order-preserving, or order-reversing relative to the truth, and only the reversing cases are exploitable.
layout: 4 panels in a row, left-to-right, shared axes, dotted guide lines marking exploiting pair
description: Four side-by-side line plots share the same style. The x-axis is the policy parameter theta from 0 to 1, and the y-axis is the policy value J(pi). Each panel plots a blue curve for the true model's value J1 and a red curve for the world model's value J2. Panel (a) has a flat red line, so the model is trivial. Panel (b) has both curves rising, so the policy ordering is preserved and the models are equivalent. Panels (c) and (d) mark two policies, pi and pi', with dots on both curves, joined by dotted grey vertical lines and faded horizontal guides. In (c) the red curve dips while the blue rises. In (d) the red curve falls while the blue rises and the curves cross. Panel titles use blue and red colored math symbols for T1 and T2. The eye goes first to the crossing and diverging curves in (c) and (d).
caption: Taxonomy of transition model relationships in a 3-state MDP ([ref]). Policies are parameterized by $\pi_\theta(a_0 \mid s) = \theta$ for all $s \in \cS$. Each panel has the same $\cT_1$ but a unique $\cT_2$. (a) $\cT_2$ is trivial, so $J_2$ is constant. (b) $\cT_1$, $\cT_2$ are equivalent (in policy ordering): both value functions increase in $\theta$, preserving the policy ordering. (c, d) $\cT_1$, $\cT_2$ are exploitable: dotted lines show the exploiting pair $(\pi, \pi')$ from [ref], with $J_1(\pi') > J_1(\pi)$ but $J_2(\pi) > J_2(\pi')$.
abstract: We propose a novel definition of model exploitation in reinforcement learning. Informally, a world model is exploitable if it implies that one policy should be strictly preferred over another while the environment's true transition model implies the reverse. We analogize our definition with a prior characterization of reward hacking but show that the associated proof of inevitability does not transfer to exploitation. To overcome this obstruction, we develop a general theory of reward hacking and model exploitation that proves that exploitation is essentially unavoidable on large policy sets and yields the corresponding claim for hacking as a special case. Unfortunately, we also find that the conditions that guarantee unhackability in finite policy sets have no counterpart that precludes exploitation. Consequently, we introduce a relaxed notion of exploitation and derive a safe horizon within which it can be avoided. Taken together, our results establish a formal bridge between reward hacking and model exploitation and elucidate the limits of safe planning in world models.
